ap_physics_1-m01.stem: Four wheels each speed up from rest with a constant angular acceleration (angular acceleration, radius of the wheel): A: angular acceleration $3\text{ rad/s}^2$, radius $0.20\text{ m}$; B: angular acceleration $6\text{ rad/s}^2$, radius $0.30\text{ m}$; C: angular acceleration $2\text{ rad/s}^2$, radius $0.40\text{ m}$; D: angular acceleration $5\text{ rad/s}^2$, radius $0.10\text{ m}$. Rank the magnitudes of the tangential acceleration of a point on the rim of each wheel from greatest to least.

options.why: Ranks by the radius alone.
Ranks by the angular acceleration alone.
The tangential acceleration is $a_t=\alpha r$, so the values are A: 0.600 m/s$^2$, B: 1.80 m/s$^2$, C: 0.800 m/s$^2$, D: 0.500 m/s$^2$, which ranks as B > C > A > D.
Ranks by $\alpha/r$, dividing by the radius instead of multiplying.

ap_physics_1-m02.stem: Two carts of equal mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ at rest on a frictionless track are pushed apart by a compressed spring between them. The spring releases a total of $6\text{ J}$ of energy, which becomes kinetic energy of the carts, and the carts have equal kinetic energy because their masses are equal: $3.00\text{ J}$ each. In a second trial one of the carts is replaced by a cart with $2$ times the mass, and the spring releases the same $6\text{ J}$. What is the best prediction of the kinetic energy of the lighter cart in the second trial?

options.why: Gives all of the energy to the lighter cart.
Momentum is conserved, so $mv_1=(2m)v_2$ and $v_1=2v_2$. The kinetic energies are in the ratio $K_1:K_2=2:1$, so the lighter cart has the fraction $2/(2+1)$ of $6\text{ J}$, which is $4.00\text{ J}$.
Gives the lighter cart the inverse share, $E/(1+f)$.
Gives the lighter cart the same share as before, ignoring the larger mass of the other cart.

ap_physics_1-m03.stem: In a hydraulic lift a small piston of area $2\text{ cm}^2$ is pushed down with a force of $20\text{ N}$ through a distance of $0.3\text{ m}$. The incompressible fluid transmits the pressure to a large piston of area $20\text{ cm}^2$. Friction is negligible. Which statement about the work done on the small piston and by the fluid on the large piston is correct and best justified?

options.text: The work done on the large piston is less than the work done on the small piston, because the fluid loses energy transmitting the force.
options.why: Assumes that energy is lost in the fluid even though friction is negligible and the fluid is incompressible.

options.text: The work done on the large piston is $10$ times as great, because the force on it is $10$ times as great.
options.why: Multiplies the work by the force factor without noticing that the large piston moves a proportionally smaller distance.

options.text: The work done on the small piston is $10$ times as great, because the small piston must be pushed with more pressure.
options.why: Confuses the pressure in the fluid with the force; the pressure is the same on both pistons.

options.text: The work is the same for both pistons, $6.00\text{ J}$, because the large piston gets a force $10$ times as great but moves only $1/10$ of the distance, so the force and distance changes cancel.
options.why: The pressure is equal, so $F_2=200\text{ N}$; the fluid volume is conserved, so $d_2=d_1/10=0.0300\text{ m}$; then $W_2=F_2d_2=6.00\text{ J}=W_1$.
